scenes.narration: Strip Lord Jim of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Lord Jim is a novel by Joseph Conrad originally published as a serial in Blackwood's Magazine from October 1899 to November 1900. An early and primary event in the story is the abandonment of a passenger ship in distress by its crew, including a young British seaman named Jim.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Lord Jim shows exactly where that breaks. He is publicly censured for this action and the novel follows his later attempts at coming to terms with himself and his past and seeking redemption and acceptance. In 1998 the Modern Library ranked Lord Jim 85th on its list of the 100 best English-language novels of the 20th century.

What looks like free choice in Lord Jim is older than choice itself. Recovering from an injury, Jim seeks a position on the SS Patna, a steamer serving the transport of 800 "pilgrims of an exacting belief" to a port on the Red Sea. After some days of smooth sailing, the ship hits something in the night and the bulkhead begins bulging under the waterline.

Nobody designed the part of Lord Jim you experience — it was inherited. Captain Gustav thinks the ship will quickly sink, and Jim agrees but wants to put the passengers on the few boats before that can happen. The captain and two other crewmen think only to save themselves, and prepare to lower a boat.

Every serious account of Lord Jim eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. The helmsmen remain, as no order has been given to do otherwise. In a crucial moment, Jim jumps into the boat with the captain.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Lord Jim — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. A few days later, they are picked up by an outbound steamer. When they reach port, they learn that the Patna and its passengers were brought in safely by a crew from a French navy ship.

The selfish-gene reading of Lord Jim makes it less romantic and far more precise. The captain's actions in abandoning both ship and passengers are against the code of the sea, and the crew is publicly vilified. When the other men leave town before the magistrate's court can be convened, Jim is the only crew member left to testify.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Brierly, a captain of perfect reputation who is on the panel of the court, inexplicably commits suicide days after the trial. Captain Charles Marlow attends the trial and meets Jim, whose behaviour he condemns, but the young man intrigues him.

The feeling that Lord Jim means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Wracked with guilt, Jim confesses his shame to Marlow, who finds him a place to live in a friend's home. Jim is accepted there but leaves abruptly when an engineer who had also abandoned the ship appears to work at the house.

Nothing in Lord Jim was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Jim then finds work as a ship chandler's clerk in ports of the East Indies, always succeeding in the job then leaving abruptly when the memory of the Patna incident catches up with him. Marlow realises that Jim needs a new situation, something that will take him far away from modern ports and keep him occupied so that he can finally forget his guilt.

The psychology underneath Lord Jim is simpler and older than the story on top. Marlow consults his friend Stein, who sees that Jim is a romantic and considers his situation. Stein offers Jim to be his trade representative or factor in Patusan, a village on a remote island shut off from most commerce, which Jim finds to be exactly what he needs.

Behind Lord Jim sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. After his initial challenge of entering the settlement of native Malay and Bugis people, Jim manages to earn their respect by relieving them of the depredations of the bandit Sherif Ali and protecting them from the corrupt local Malay chief, Rajah Tunku Allang. He builds a solid link with Doramin, the Bugis friend of Stein, and his son Dain Waris.

The nihilist does not deny Lord Jim — he only refuses to flatter it. For his leadership, the people call him "Tuan Jim", or Lord Jim. Jim also wins the love of Jewel, a young woman of mixed race, and is "satisfied... nearly." Marlow visits Patusan once, two years after Jim arrived there, and sees his success.

What culture calls destiny in Lord Jim is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Jewel does not believe that Jim will stay, as her father left her mother, and she is not reassured that Marlow or any other outsider will not arrive to take him from her. Her mother had been married before her death to Cornelius, previously given the factor's role by Stein for her benefit.

The genes do not care about Lord Jim; they care about copies. Cornelius is a lazy, jealous, and brutal man who treats his stepdaughter cruelly and steals the supplies Stein sends for sale; he is displaced by Jim's arrival and resents him for it. "Gentleman" Brown, a marauding captain notorious for his evil ways, then sails into Patusan, his small crew on the brink of starvation.

Take away the meaning and Lord Jim still functions — that is the disturbing part. The local defence led by Dain Waris manages to prevent the marauders from looting the village and holds them entrenched in place while Jim is away in the island's interior. When Jim returns and Brown deceptively wins Jim's mercy, Jim hesitantly negotiates to allow them to leave Patusan unobstructed, but reminds Brown that the long passage down river to the sea will be guarded by armed men.

The unconscious does not argue with Lord Jim; it simply acts first. He tells Brown of a side channel that will bypass most of the defences, which Brown navigates, stopping briefly to ambush the defenders he finds out of revenge. Dain Waris is killed, among others, and Brown sails on, leaving Cornelius behind.

Lord Jim feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Jim is mortified when he receives word of the death of his good friend Waris. He resigns himself to his earlier commitment that no villagers would be harmed and chooses not to flee.

The bleak reading of Lord Jim is also the most testable one. Jewel, who had wanted Jim to attack Brown and his ship, is distraught and begs him to defend himself and never leave her. Jim then goes directly to Doramin and in front of the village takes responsibility for the death of his only son.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Lord Jim. Devastated, Doramin uses his flintlock pistols, given him by Stein, to execute Jim by shooting him in the chest. On his regular route, Marlow arrives at Stein's house a few days after this event, finding Jewel and Tamb' Itam there, and tries to make sense of what happened.

The self that experiences Lord Jim is a committee, not a king. Jewel stays under the protection of Stein, who presages his own death. Marlow: A sea captain in the Merchant Navy who helps Jim after his fall from grace, trying to understand how "one of us" could lack the bravery and judgment expected of seamen.

Reproduction explains more of Lord Jim than any philosophy dares to admit. Marlow is also the narrator of three of Conrad's other works: Heart of Darkness, Youth, and Chance. Jim: Young parson's son who takes to the sea, training for the merchant service as steam ships mix with sailing ships.

Once you see Lord Jim as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Captain Gustav: Captain of the Patna, an Australian born in Germany, who is interested in the money made from this ship, with no concern for his honour as a captain. After learning ashore that the ship came in ahead of them, he knows his certificate will be cancelled and he leaves, never seen again.

The story Lord Jim tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Ship's engineers: Three men who keep the steam boiler working; one is George, who dies of a heart attack on the Patna as the others leave the ship. Another shows up later by chance at the same place where Jim is living, driving Jim away.

Meaning is not found in Lord Jim — it is manufactured for it. He sits in the court that hears the case of the Patna crew, telling Marlow that Jim ought to hide somewhere, as he can never work as a seaman again. A few days after the trial, this superior man ("indeed, had you been Emperor of East and West, you could not have ignored your inferiority in his presence", Chapter 6) kills himself by jumping off his ship at sea, leaving no explanation.

The cold light on Lord Jim leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Stein: Head of Stein & Co., friend of Marlow, and a man with a long, interesting life. He has had success in trade in the East, collecting produce from various ports in the Dutch colonial areas and settling far from his native Bavaria after losing in the uprisings of 1848.

Lord Jim did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. He learned lepidopterology, which became his passionate hobby, gaining him a reputation for all the specimens he sent to contacts in Europe in this age of scientific discovery. Jewel: Daughter of a Dutch-Malay woman and a white European man, never named, who deserted them.

The honest version of Lord Jim starts by giving up the comforting part. Cornelius: Former factor for Stein & Co., on account of his wife, whom Stein admired. When replaced by Jim, he does not leave the area, nor does he find any useful occupation for himself.

Strip Lord Jim of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. He connives with the marauder Brown to kill Jim, succeeding indirectly after Brown's men kill Dain Waris. Cornelius is killed by Tamb' Itam, who sees him after the attack and realizes the role he played.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Lord Jim shows exactly where that breaks. Doramin: Old chief of the Bugis people in Patusan and father of Dain Waris, his only son. He was a friend to Stein, and the two exchanged gifts on parting: Doramin gave a ring to Stein, and Stein gave pistols to Doramin.

What looks like free choice in Lord Jim is older than choice itself. Dain Waris: The only son of Doramin; a young, strong, and fiercely devoted leader of his people. Sherif Ali: Local bandit who is a trial to all others in Patusan, extorting fees and stealing crops and resources from others.

Nobody designed the part of Lord Jim you experience — it was inherited. Rajah Tunku Allang: Malay chief in Patusan who took Jim prisoner on his first entry into the country. Gentleman Brown: A cruel captain of a latter-day pirate crew, who kills because he can, and is not a success in life.

Every serious account of Lord Jim eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. He has a ship in poor condition and a crew of men similar to him when he runs short of food near Patusan. He goes up the river to the village, which successfully forces him to retreat to a nearby hilltop.
